chapter_theme: Things as they truly are (மெய்ம்மை): the hard facts of the world, as opposed to how people would like it to be. Natures do not change, kin come with fortune and leave with it, the rich are heard and the poor are not, and in the end only one's deeds go with one.
structure_note: Unlike the chapter title's usual sense of truthfulness, only 111 concerns keeping one's word. The rest is a run of observations about how the world works, several framed as facts no one can alter (112, 116) and one as four rhetorical questions (119). The chapter closes on death (120), echoing chapter 11.

111.reading: Saying 'I have none' about something one cannot give is no disgrace and is the way of the world; but keeping someone waiting till their hope dies and then failing them is a worse fault than killing a kindness received.
111.nuance: The verse doesn't fault refusal; it faults the false promise that turns refusal into torment. Both commentators read கொன்றாரின் as a comparison, worse than ingratitude, where Pope says only 'like'.

112.reading: The worthy and the unworthy never fall away from their own natures: jaggery is not bitter whoever eats it, and neem is bitter even if gods eat it.
112.nuance: The claim runs both ways: circumstances cannot spoil the good, and they cannot redeem the bad. The gods are named to say that even the highest eater does not change the taste.

113.reading: When a man prospers, kin who cling to him are more numerous than the stars that move in the sky; when unbearable trouble strikes, few say 'we are related to him', lord of the cool hills.
113.nuance: Mudaliar notes that கிளைஞர் means, by its root, those who cling like branches, which sharpens the irony of their leaving.

114.reading: Of the three that endure in this world, whoever gains the middle one gains both ends as well; whoever does not gains a suffering like being boiled in a furnace.
114.nuance: The verse doesn't name the three; both commentators identify them as virtue, wealth and pleasure, with wealth in the middle. For a work that elsewhere calls wealth unreliable, this is a strong statement of its worth. Pope's turtle in the pot is his own; Mudaliar has a smith's furnace.

115.reading: Even a young calf fetches a price if its mother is a good cow, and the words of the rich are accepted even if they are unlearned; the words of the poor glance off like a plough in barely moist soil.
115.nuance: The calf image says worth is borrowed from the source, not earned; the plough image says the poor man's words do not sink in. The verse reports this as how things are, not as how they should be.

116.reading: Those without restraint stay unrestrained even if they study true wisdom widely, as a wild bitter gourd stays bitter though cooked with salt, ghee, milk, curd and asafoetida.
116.nuance: Mudaliar takes அடங்காதார் as those who are by nature not given to restraint, so the point is that learning cannot change a nature, not that learning is useless.

117.reading: Scorn those who scorn you, before they do; what have you to do with them? What is bound to come comes to everyone, lord of the shore fragrant with punnai flowers.
117.nuance: The link between the advice and the last line is not stated. One reading is that since what is fated will come anyway, there is nothing to lose by answering scorn. Mudaliar takes அவரின் முன் either as at the very moment they scorn or to their faces rather than behind their backs, and calls the verse a way to silence groundless slanderers.

118.reading: Cows differ in colour, but the milk they give does not; virtue, like milk, is of one nature, while its ways here take many forms, like the cows.
118.nuance: Mudaliar takes the many ways as the many means of practising one virtue. Pope makes them the schools or sects that teach it, which turns the verse into a statement about religious diversity; the Tamil says only நெறி.

119.reading: Who in the world has escaped having a word said against them? Who has not lived by stratagem? Who has not met hardship midway? Who has kept their wealth to the end?
119.nuance: The four questions expect the answer 'no one', so the verse states the common lot without saying it. Mudaliar gives two senses of உபாயம்: the four political stratagems, or the ordinary means of livelihood.

120.reading: Search where you will, nothing goes with a person but the deeds they have done; even the body they guarded and adorned is of no use when Death seizes it and runs.
120.nuance: வினை here is not only good deeds: what goes along can be a burden as well as a support.

links.note: The Kural makes killing a kindness received the sin with no escape. On both commentators' reading, 111 names something worse: a promise held out and then broken.
223 praises never uttering 'I have nothing' and giving instead. 111 allows that saying 'no' is blameless when one truly cannot give; the fault lies in false promising.

112 says the worthy and unworthy never fall from their natures at any time. 514 says that many people, though trusted after every test, change through the nature of the work. The tension holds if 514 means people really change, as Parimelazhagar says, rather than that the tests misjudged them.
113 observes that kin vanish in trouble; 796 turns that into a benefit, saying ruin is a rod that measures one's people.
Both say that whoever secures wealth gets the other two aims of life as well. The Naladiyar adds the cost of failing: suffering like being boiled.

114 makes wealth the key to virtue and pleasure; 1, opening the book, shows the rich reduced to begging for gruel and says wealth should not be counted on. Wealth secures the other two only while it lasts.
Both say that the poor are not heard however sound their words. The Naladiyar adds the other half: the rich are heard even when unlearned.
Both describe study that leaves a person unrestrained. The Kural calls such a person the greatest fool; the Naladiyar says it is their nature, as bitterness is the gourd's.

117 says to scorn those who scorn you; 151 says that bearing with them, as the earth bears those who dig it, is the highest thing. Both concern the same situation. The tension depends on reading 117 as advice, as Mudaliar, Shanmuganar and Pope do, and not as irony.

Within the Naladiyar: 72 says that when unworthy people speak improperly, bearing it in silence is fitting and the world thinks retaliation shameful. 117 says to scorn the scorners first. The tension holds if 117's scorners and 72's speakers are the same kind of person.
118 says virtue is one in nature whatever form its ways take. 34 says what that one thing is: a spotless mind, everything else being show.
36 makes virtue the companion that does not die with you. 120 says the only thing that goes along is the deed, which includes bad deeds; so the companion can also be a burden.

source_issues: Shanmuganar's verse numbers in this chapter run 41 to 50, and 120's Shanmuganar field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
